power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 10 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: There are many different data analytical procedures applicable to data obtained via single-case experimental designs, with mean differences, regression-based procedures, and nonoverlap indices being among the most frequently used ones.
The possibilities are reduced when the data are ordinal and/or variable and cannot be meaningfully summarized by straight lines.
For such scenarios, nonoverlap indices become prominent.
The current text is a continuation of previous discussions related to the quantification of trend in the context of using nonoverlap indices.
Focusing on the Tau indices by Parker and colleagues and by Tarlow, we underline potential drawbacks that have not been discussed previously, while also suggesting alternatives.

Specifically, we point at situations in which underestimation and overestimation of trend are possible, as well as discussing the quantification problems arising in case trend levels off by reaching an upper or lower bound.

The aim of the review of existing options and of the tentatively proposed alternatives is to ignite further discussion regarding how to deal with trend without assuming that a straight line (or any specific nonlinear model) is a good representation of the data.
A new graphical representation is suggested to accompany the newly proposed quantification of monotonic trend.
Single-case experimental designs allow obtaining evidence on whether an intervention is effective, on the basis of multiple measurements of the target behavior in different conditions.

The term "ordinal" refers to the measurement scale of the dependent variable, considering how information is gathered.
Specifically, ordinal data only allow for saying whether two values are equal or not (like in a nominal scale) and, if not, which value is larger.

They do not justify quantifications in terms of distance due to the impossibility to assume constant distances or intervals between pairs of possible values (i.e., the data cannot be assumed to be measured in an interval scale).
Ordinal data can arise, for instance, from rating scales representing subjective states (e.g., satisfaction, fatigue).

text.text: Such a progression entails that there is no stable or maintained level in a given condition, but rather a change is taking place in subsequent measurement occasions.
A trend can take place in the baseline and represent a deterioration or a spontaneous improvement before an intervention is introduced.
A trend can also take place in the intervention phase, indicating that the effect of the intervention is progressive rather than abrupt and maintained.

Before referring to the existing proposals for combining nonoverlap and monotonic trend, it is important to define two terms.
The first term is "monotonic trend"
and it refers to a progression in the data in which the direction does not change.
Specifically, if the measurements are increasing at earlier moments, they never decrease at later moments (i.e., they only increase or are maintained equal to adjacent previous measurements).
Analogously, if the measurements are decreasing at earlier moments, they never increase at later moments (i.e., they only decrease or are maintained equal to adjacent previous measurements).
This definition of trend is present in Tau-U (Parker, Vannest, David, & Sauber, 2011) and in the Baseline corrected Tau (BCT; Tarlow, 2017).

text.text: In relation to trend, a second term that needs to be defined is "strictly monotonic trend", which we recommend in the current text, as will be discussed later.
A "strictly monotonic trend" is a progression in which the measurements in a given phase always change in the same direction without maintaining equal values.

Specifically, if the measurements are increasing at earlier moments, they only increase at later moments (i.e., they do not decrease and do not remain the same as in the adjacent previous measurement).

Analogously, if the measurements are decreasing at earlier moments, they only decrease at later moments (i.e., they do not increase and do not remain the same as in the adjacent previous measurement).

In these data there is no clear trend: accordingly, three quantifications agree in assigning 0 to baseline trend: (a) Kendall's correlation incorporated in BCT; (b) monotonic trend as quantified in Tau-U; and (c) the strictly monotonic trend as quantified via β A .
In contrast, the Theil-Sen estimate is -0.13.
Thus, there is a contradiction not only with other quantifications of trend, but also within the two quantifications of trend that are part of BCT.
This example illustrates a potential limitation of BCT and a reason why we advocate for NAP, reflecting better the visual impression.

As mentioned previously, Tau-U (Parker, Vannest, Sauber, & Davis, 2011) compares each measurement to all of the previous measurement from the same condition, regardless of how far away in time they are obtained.
text.formatted: As mentioned previously, Tau-U <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Parker, Vannest, Sauber, & Davis, 2011)</ref> compares each measurement to all of the previous measurement from the same condition, regardless of how far away in time they are obtained.

text.text: There are two consequences.
First, an earlier measurement is involved in more comparisons than later measurements and, thus, can have greater effect on the quantification of trend.

This may be especially problematic if researchers wait for an initially variable baseline to stabilize before intervening: the quantification of trend will be highly influenced by the values prior to stabilizing.
Second, an outlier can distort the comparisons with all subsequent measurements, when quantifying monotonic trend.
In contrast, the definition of strictly monotonic trend in β A entails comparing only adjacent values.
Therefore, all measurements, except for the first and the last in the phase, have influence on two within-phase comparisons only -when comparing to the previous and to the subsequent value.

Regarding the justification of the focus on adjacent values, it is strongly related to how differencing is performed in ARIMA models (Harrop & Velicer, 1985) and also to the mean phase difference quantification (Manolov & Solanas, 2013).

text.text: Visual inspection suggests that the baseline could be considered stable, except for the first lower measurement, or stabilized after the first measurement.

Tau-U's quantification of monotonic trend does not reflect this impression of stability, as the value is .40, leading to a corrected nonoverlap value of .77, compared to the uncorrected one of .89 and NAP of .94.
Similarly, Kendall's correlation from BCT also seems to entail an overestimation of baseline trend yielding a value of .632.

This entails a contradiction within BCT (opposite to the contradiction from the first example in which Kendall's correlation was 0, but the Theil-Sen estimate was not).
The quantification of strictly monotonic trend is β A = .25 , which is less pronounced that the quantifications from Tau-U and Kendall's correlation, and better aligned with the visual impression.
Considering baseline stability, we could argue for using NAP for quantifying nonoverlap.
This would avoid underestimating the effect due to excessive trend correction in Tau-U or due to lack of certainty whether BCT actually quantifies overlap.

text.text: For such a pattern as the one observed during the intervention phase, the quantification of strictly monotonic trend could be underestimated (the value of β B = .33 ).
This quantification is potentially affected by the fact that the measurements cannot increase any more.
Thus, a stopping rule may be justified.

Specifically, when quantifying strictly monotonic trend, it would be reasonable to exclude the data (and the comparisons) after the upper bound is achieved and after it is verified via visual inspection that this asymptote is maintained in subsequent measurements.
In this specific example, if we discard the last two intervention phase measurements, β B = .50 , correcting the underestimation.
For the sake of illustrating the effect of an asymptote, in case the increase continued (if we substitute the last two 10s of the intervention phase with the values of 11 and 12, β B would be .67).

However, the β B value with the stopping rule is still lower than the monotonic trend quantification from Tau-U (equal to 0.71 when using all data and equal to .70 when discarding the last two intervention phase measurements), because the latter performs more comparisons, specifically to earlier (and lower) intervention phase values.

Still, the measurements obtained once the upper asymptote is reached also make the monotonic trend quantification of Tau-U smaller, that what it would have been in case the increase continued (if we substitute the last two 10s of the intervention phase with the values of 11 and 12, the quantification of monotonic trend would be .86).

text.text: As an interpretative challenge, taking into account the trends in the baseline and intervention phase, a comparison in level is only possible for a given moment in time (e.g., the first or the last intervention phase measurement occasion) not overall.
Actually, such a comparison implicitly entails a projection of baseline trend.
In contrast, the comparison between the estimates of slope in baseline and intervention phase entails no projection.
We here suggest not to account for trend, but rather to assess whether it is present and act accordingly quantifying it.
Instead of suggesting a quantification of overlap for a given moment in time, we suggest using NAP when there is no trend.

On the contrary, when there is trend, we recommend comparing the monotonic trends in the baseline and intervention phase (i.e., the values of β A and β B ), as would be done when comparing slopes in a piecewise regression model.

Similarly, we do not suggest extending baseline trend, although this would allow for a comparison between actual and projected data, as suggested by Kratochwill et al. (2013), and as feasible via PEM-T (Wolery et al., 2010) or the regression model by Swaminathan et al. (2014).

text.text: The following examples were specifically tailored by us (i.e., they were not extracted from previous publications) in order to represent different ways in which (potentially) random fluctuations can be expressed in the data.
The data and the quantifications are presented in Table 1.

text.text: The first example of the data within the same phase, includes five measurements: 6,7,6,7, and 6.
Apparently, there is only random (alternating) fluctuation around a stable level.
All quantifications of trend (from Tau-U, BCT, and beta) coincide in yielding the value of 0.
The second example is similar, but without the last measurement: only 6, 7, 6, and 7.
For these data, all four quantifications yield a positive result (with Kendall's correlation being highest and the Theil-Sen estimate being lowest).
Given that the first measurement is lower and the last is higher, a positive quantification might make sense.
However, from such a short series how can the researcher be confident that there is something more than random fluctuation?
The third and the fourth examples are similar among themselves, with three out of four values being equal and one value in the middle being different.
If the data were 6, 7, 6, and 6, Tau-U's quantification of trend and Kendall's correlation would be positive, whereas beta and the Theil-Sen estimate are zero.
The latter could be considered to better represent stability.
Complementarily, if the data were 6, 6, 7, and 6, Tau-U's quantification of trend and Kendall's correlation would be positive, whereas beta and the Theil-Sen estimate are zero.
It may not be desirable for the position of the only different value to determine to such an extent the quantification of trend, if this position is not at either of the extremes of the data series.
Regarding extremes, if the data were 6, 6, 6, and 7, all quantifications would reflect the larger last value with positive values for trend.
The trend from Tau-U and Kendall's correlation seems to represent an overestimation, considering that there is only different value from the series of four measurements.
Complementarily, if the data were 7, 6, 6, and 6, all quantifications would reflect the larger first value with negative values for trend.
For these data, given the increased stability at the end of the baseline, trend quantifications closer to 0 would be desirable.

These examples suggest that in certain situations the quantification of monotonic trend via Tau-U and Kendall's correlation (which is part of the BCT) can be an overestimation (i.e., yielding a value farther away from zero than warranted).

Nonetheless, the examples provide no definitive evidence for superiority of either procedure, although they do point at the importance of having enough data in order to be able to assess with greater confidence whether there is something more than random fluctuations in the data.
As part of the proposal for defining strictly monotonic trend, a new graphical representation is suggested, illustrated in the right panels of Figures 1, 2, and 3.

text.text: This graph would represent the differences between successive measures within each phase, consistent with the definition of monotonic trend.
When the differences are in the direction of improvement, they are marked with green dots.
Complementarily, when the differences entail deterioration, they are marked with red dots.
Ties are marked in blue.
A predominance of green dots would reflect an overall trend of improvement.

According to where these green dots are located in time, it is possible to evaluate whether there is a strictly monotonic trend throughout the whole phase or the data pattern is somewhat more complex (e.g., a monotonic trend that has late onset or that fades away).

If there are more green dots (proportionately to the number of measurements) in the intervention phase than in the baseline phase, this would be indicative of a stronger improving trend after the intervention.
Moreover, in case the lower or upper bound is reached, and the quantification of strictly monotonic trend ceases, the remaining data points are marked in grey (not in green, red, or blue).
We consider that the topic discussed in the current text is relevant and the debate is necessary, due to five reasons.
First, nonoverlap indices and monotonic trend are useful quantifications when data are ordinal and/or variable and cannot be reasonably summarized by (i.e., reduced to) a mean or straight trend line.

text.text: As the aim of the current text is to ignite discussion, beyond the alternatives suggested, there are still many questions that need to be answered.
We here specifically comment on two such questions next: the need for modeling and the place of inference in SCED data analysis.
NAP and Tau use the measurements as obtained when performing calculations.
These measurements are not reduced by any summary measure (e.g., there is no comparison between a baseline mean and an intervention phase mean).
The same is the case when quantifying monotonic trend (as operationally defined in Tau-U) and strictly monotonic trend (as operationally defined here).
In that sense, all these calculations could be said to be sensitive to chance fluctuations.

On the one hand, chance fluctuations can be relevant for the quantification of trend, as shown previously in the text (see the subsection entitled "Random fluctuations (or not)" within the "Issues and Suggested Alternatives" section).
On the other hand, they can have an effect on baseline trend control.
For instance, when deciding whether to control for baseline trend, Parker, Vannest, Davis, and Sauber's (2011) recommend assessing whether trend is pronounced or credible.
text.formatted: For instance, when deciding whether to control for baseline trend, <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Parker, Vannest, Davis, and Sauber's (2011)</ref> recommend assessing whether trend is pronounced or credible.

text.text: Accordingly, Lee and Cherney (2018) illustrating Tau-U, chose a cut-off point for baseline trend control that corresponds to "trend that is evident upon visual inspection of the data" (p. 498).

Such a way of proceeding leads to a subjective judgment which may be suboptimal or not necessarily rational (e.g., consider the results by Henderson et al., 2006, on participants giving more or less importance to deviations when assessing trend according to irrelevant factors, illustrating the Construal Level Theory).

text.text: Moreover, it has been emphasized that with short series it can be difficult to determine whether there are trends: on the one hand, an existing trend may not be detected and, on the other hand, a small sample of observations may suggest that data appear to have trend (Wolfe & Ferron, 2026).

text.text: In this context, we should consider also the human tendency to look for deterministic patterns even when there are not any (see Kahneman et al., 2021, and psychological traps such as the post-hoc causal narrative and the denial of statistical reality).

text.text: Thus, the researchers' knowledge about the participant and the relevant variables surrounding the intervention and the target behavior can be crucial for distinguishing between pattern and random (unexplained) variability.
The alternative would be to try to represent the real underlying pattern via a model and thus reduce noise.
For instance, regression-based models include such representations of the data via trend lines and the standardized mean difference does the same via mean lines.
The descriptive measures require assuming or checking that these lines fit well the data, whereas any inferential information requires further assumptions about the results.
Moreover, it is not always clear whether we can imagine that a model is correct only because it fits well the data.
For instance, a quadratic model can fit well to exponential data but still be incorrect, just like a cubic model can fit well to logistic data but still be incorrect.
Additionally, there may not be any solid rationale (from previous evidence or from the data gathered) for any given model.
We specifically contextualized the discussion of overlap and trend in scenarios in which data are not stable.
We do not have an answer to the questions whether data variability is noise (unwanted chance fluctuation) or it is information worth keeping in its original form.
We consider that this question cannot be answered in general, irrespective of the knowledge of the person, issue treated, and intervention.

Therefore, we consider that a parsimonious option would be to work directly with the data (as in NAP, Tau-U, and the definitions of monotonic and strictly monotonic trend), rather than using models to account for or reduce chance fluctuations.

The focus here is put on descriptive quantifications (i.e., how actually obtained measurements are summarized in order to assess intervention effectiveness), rather than on inferential procedures.

Regarding inference in general, we advocate for design-based tentative causal inference (such as the one made possible by randomization tests; Onghena, 2020), rather than model-based population inference, which may not be of real interest for SCED researchers.
